extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students, writers, and scholars studying narrative theory (general readers of fiction and criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evaluative vocabulary for analyzing and producing narrative (fiction and other narrative forms), focusing on distinctions such as story vs discourse, event types, temporal manipulation, gaps, conflict/closure, themes, truth-claims, and adaptation. Intended to guide literary analysis and craft decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs Narrative discourse (core distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Story: the sequence of events as the reader reconstructs them"; "Narrative discourse: the actual telling — order, framing, voice, focalization."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental evaluative axis: every narrative has a story (chronological events) and a discourse (how those events are presented). Assessments should distinguish clarity/coherence of the underlying story from the richness, order, voice, focalization, and techniques of the discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent vs Supplementary events
rubrics_metrics.description: "Constituent events: those that must occur for the story to work; remove them and the story collapses"; "Supplementary events: those that add thematic, atmospheric, or characterological weight but could be removed without breaking the plot."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the text preserves constituent integrity while using supplementary events to enrich theme, atmosphere, and characterization. A praised achievement is using supplementary events generously without losing constituent integrity; penalize unnecessary supplementary material that undermines plot economy or focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative time (story time, discourse time, reading time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three temporal dimensions: story time — the chronological order of events; discourse time — the order in which they are narrated; reading time — the time spent reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the author manipulates these temporal dimensions. Mismatches among them create effects (flashback, foreshadowing, suspense, surprise). Judge appropriateness, clarity, and effect of temporal displacements and pacing relative to intended experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative gaps (constituent vs supplementary gaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every narrative has gaps — what is left unsaid that the reader must fill. Two types: constituent gaps — withholding what is needed for the story (mystery, suspense); supplementary gaps — leaving out detail that the reader fills with imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the strategic placement of gaps: whether withheld information builds mystery/suspense (constituent gaps) or invites imaginative participation/texture (supplementary gaps). Good craft is the art of strategic gap placement; poor craft either withholds too much (confusing) or too little (over-explicit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict and closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives proceed via conflict — opposition between characters, between desires, between facts and beliefs. Closure resolves (or refuses to resolve) the conflict. Open endings are choices, not failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the central conflicts' clarity and stakes, and evaluate the chosen form of closure (resolving, partial, or open). Consider whether an open ending is thematically and formally justified rather than merely inconclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themes and motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: "Theme: the work's general intellectual or moral content"; "Motif: a recurring image, phrase, or event that builds the theme."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how motifs recur and concretize thematic concerns and whether the themes emerge coherently from the narrative material. Look for economy and resonance between motif recurrence and thematic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-claims of fiction (emotional, structural, moral truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction can express truths that propositional discourse cannot — emotional truth, structural truth, moral truth. "The truth-claim of fiction is different from but not weaker than that of nonfiction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the kinds of truth the work stakes: does it achieve emotional or structural insights that feel compelling? Consider whether the fictional contract (reader's willing suspension) supports the work's truth-claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation: story vs discourse across media
rubrics_metrics.description: When narrative crosses media (novel → film), what survives is the story; what changes is the discourse. The constituent/supplementary distinction predicts which adaptations succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For adaptations, evaluate which elements are constituent (likely to survive) versus discourse choices (likely to change), and judge success by how well the adapted discourse realizes the original story's constitutive elements and preserves or reinterprets supplementary material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of narrative / narrative as sense-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative is not confined to literature, film, or theater — it is a fundamental human cognitive activity. We narrate to make sense of experience. The same narrative principles operate in dinner-table anecdotes, court testimony, news reporting, and novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess narratives for their capacity to make sense of experience across contexts. Consider applicability of narrative techniques beyond literary genres; evaluate whether techniques function coherently given the communicative context (anecdote, testimony, reportage, fiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary evaluative criteria (explicit list)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative can be analyzed on: Clarity of story vs. richness of discourse; Skillful use of supplementary events; Strategic gap placement; Coherence of themes and motifs; Truth-claim made by the fictional contract; Treatment of conflict and choice of closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list as an assessment checklist: each item names a dimension to score or discuss when evaluating a narrative's strengths and weaknesses. Combine these dimensions rather than treating any single one as exhaustive.
